Question: Let \(P\) be an interior point of circle \(K\) other than the center of \(K.\) Form all chords of \(K\) which pass through \(P,\) and determine their midpoints. The locus of these midpoints is

Choices.A: a circle with one point deleted
Choices.B:
a circle if the distance from \(P\) to the center of \(K\) is
less than one half the radius of \(K;\) otherwise a circular arc of
less than \(360^\circ\)
Choices.C: a semicircle with one point deleted

Solution:
Let \(O\) be the center of \(K\). A circle's center lies on the perpendicular bisector of every chord, which connects chord midpoints to right angles. We will show that the locus is the circle \(\Gamma\) with diameter \(OP\). Since \(P\ne O\), this is a genuine circle.

Take a chord through \(P\), and let \(M\) be its midpoint. If \(M\) differs from both \(O\) and \(P\), then \(OM\) is perpendicular to the chord. Because \(P\) and \(M\) lie on that chord,
\[
\angle OMP=90^\circ.
\]
By the converse of the diameter-angle theorem, \(M\) lies on \(\Gamma\). If \(M=O\) or \(M=P\), it is already an endpoint of the diameter of \(\Gamma\). Thus every chord midpoint lies on \(\Gamma\).

Conversely, take any point \(M\) on \(\Gamma\) other than \(O\) and \(P\). The diameter-angle theorem gives \(OM\perp PM\). Since \(P\) is inside \(K\), the line \(PM\) cuts \(K\) in a chord. The perpendicular from \(O\) to that chord meets it at \(M\), so \(M\) is its midpoint.

The endpoint \(O\) occurs as the midpoint of the diameter through \(P\). The endpoint \(P\) occurs as the midpoint of the chord through \(P\) perpendicular to \(OP\). Therefore every point of \(\Gamma\) is attained, and the locus is a complete circle, choice \(\boxed{\mathrm{E}}\).
